questions.prompt: What is the intent of the Strategy pattern?

options.text: Define a family of interchangeable algorithms so the algorithm can vary independently from clients
Let an object change behavior as its internal state changes
Capture and restore an object's state
Ensure a class has one instance

questions.explanation: Strategy makes algorithms interchangeable. Behavior changing with state = State; capture/restore = Memento; one instance = Singleton.

questions.prompt: What is the intent of the State pattern?

options.text: Allow an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes, so it appears to change its class
Provide a simplified interface to a subsystem
Select one of several interchangeable algorithms
Share intrinsic state across many objects

questions.explanation: State ties behavior to a changing internal mode. Simplify = Facade; selecting an algorithm = Strategy; sharing state = Flyweight.

questions.prompt: Strategy and State share nearly the same structure. What is the KEY difference?

options.text: Intent and who drives the change: the client picks a Strategy; a State object transitions itself as its state changes
Strategy uses inheritance and State uses composition
They have completely different class diagrams
State cannot be implemented in TypeScript

questions.explanation: Same delegation structure, different intent: choosing an algorithm (Strategy) vs behavior tied to self-transitioning state (State).

questions.prompt: In the State pattern, who usually triggers the move to the next state?

options.text: The state objects themselves — a state knows and sets the next state
The client always sets it manually, like a Strategy
A global singleton registry
The garbage collector

questions.explanation: States commonly reference and transition to other states, so the object advances on its own.

questions.prompt: Match each characteristic to the pattern it best fits.

pairs.left: Object transitions through modes over its lifetime
The parts are independent and unaware of each other
The parts often trigger transitions to one another

questions.explanation: Strategy: independent algorithms chosen by the client. State: modes that transition, often referencing each other.

questions.prompt: You're replacing a large if/else on an order's 'status' that changes over time (pending, paid, shipped). Which pattern fits?

options.text: State — the object moves through modes with different behavior
Strategy — you're just picking one algorithm once
Singleton
Flyweight

questions.explanation: A changing status with per-mode behavior and transitions is the State pattern; Strategy would be a one-time algorithm choice.
